tagline: Forest roads join the Coquille valley to the Rogue River
intro: The Rogue–Coquille Scenic Byway connects Gold Beach, Agness, Powers and Coquille through the Siskiyou National Forest. FHWA gives the byway’s length as 82.5 miles and highlights its wooded paths, geological formations and recreation along the Wild and Scenic Rogue River. The road between Gold Beach and Agness winds through the river country.

Access to the lower Rogue once depended on pack animals and a hard-won mailboat service. Elijah H. Price proposed a permanent boat route in 1883; the Post Office Department agreed to a trial in 1895. Difficult rapids still required mule or horse delivery between Illahe and Marial, and after 1908 most mail beyond Agness traveled by pack animal.

Traveling from Coquille toward Gold Beach, the town sequence runs through Myrtle Point and Powers. At Myrtle Point, the Middle Fork joins the South Fork south of town; the North Fork joins the combined river north of town. Powers Highway follows the South Fork Coquille; forest roads then connect Powers to the Rogue. Illahe lies upriver from Agness, which stands near the meeting of the Rogue and Illinois rivers. From Agness, continue down the Rogue toward Gold Beach.

moments.title: Powers
moments.text: Powers stands on the South Fork Coquille River, where the highway from Myrtle Point meets the forest-road connection to the Rogue. Oregon Geographic Names records that the town was named in 1914 for Albert H. Powers, vice president and general manager of the Smith-Powers Logging Company. The post office followed in 1915. The Wagner House stands beside a railroad museum. A Forest Service district office is on the main road, and the Siskiyou National Forest lies about five miles farther south along the byway. The town celebrates Independence Day with its White Cedar Days festival.

moments.title: Illahe
moments.text: In 1883, Elijah H. Price asked for a permanent mailboat route up the Rogue. He told the government it would serve perhaps eleven families and no towns. The Post Office Department finally approved a one-year trial in 1895, making his log cabin at Big Bend a post office and Price its unpaid trial-year postmaster. He had to ensure one boat round-trip each week. He named the office Illahe, from a Chinook Jargon word meaning land, earth or country. The post office closed in 1943. Beyond Illahe, difficult rapids required carriers to transfer mail to mules or horses for the journey to Marial.

moments.title: Agness
moments.text: Agness takes its spelling from an error: its post office was named for Agnes, the first postmaster’s daughter, and subsequently misspelled. Established in 1897, the office served a community near the meeting of the Lower Rogue and Illinois rivers. The winding road to Gold Beach helped keep a small local school in operation because of the community’s remoteness. Called a one-room school, it actually had two rooms. The building now houses the Agness Community Library. In 1969 the school had six pupils; by 2003 it had four students, a teacher and an aide.
